articleTitle: Stereo origination, sound pick-up and stereo post production techniques
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Stereo Sound for Television
abstract: Summary form only given. Describes the factors to be taken into consideration when making stereo television programmes and the requirements for cost effective production. Various microphone arrangements and sound balancing techniques are described and some analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of each given. The application of these techniques to real programmes is discussed and illustrated with examples from a variety of recent BBC Television programmes. Reference is made to methods of deriving monophonic signals from stereo sources and the implications of various microphone techniques on monophonic compatibility are discussed. The history of television audio post production work and the development of techniques to cope with the ever increasing complexity of production methods are reviewed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dual channel sound at Channel Four (TV station)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Stereo Sound for Television
abstract: Channel Four is a national TV network, broadcasting on average 20 hours per day. The addition of a second level of audio presented a wide variety of problems and has involved a major rebuild of in-house facilities and distribution systems as well as the incorporation of larger central routing and network switching systems. These major changes were complicated by the need to convert both main and standby presentation mixers plus the MCR emergency switcher to stereo; equip incoming and outgoing BT lines with DCS equipment and install stereo processing units on the output of every VTR.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Stereo Sound for Television
abstract: The BBC is planning to provide a television stereo sound service to 70% of the population by September 1991. Crystal Palace, which serves some 12% of the population has been radiating test transmissions for two years now, providing much valuable experience on the practical implementation of a stereo service. By the September 1991 date it is intended that ten high power main stations will have been re-engineered and be capable of carrying a stereo service. These ten stations together with their attendant relays will serve an estimated 74% of the population.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Future developments of the NICAM 728 system
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Stereo Sound for Television
abstract: There is much potential for the future development of the NICAM 728 system. The system could easily be adapted to work both with other terrestrial television transmission systems and PAL-based DBS services. The data transmission capabilities of the existing baseband coding specification have yet to be fully explored. Two areas, where significant benefits could be gained in the future, are in the development of options for multichannel sound channels, suitable for enhance television services and the introduction of conditional access scrambling. These would require new baseband coding options to be specified for the NICAM system which would, necessarily, be incompatible with existing decoder circuits. Therefore, if such coding options are developed, they will require a new generations of decoder circuits capable of dealing with both the existing and the new baseband coding options. As extensions to the existing system specification, any new coding options should, if possible, form the basis of internationally agreed specifications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital audio in the TV studio centre
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Stereo Sound for Television
abstract: The system described is well advanced in its implementation and together with the new generation of digital PCM VTRs will provide a state of the art programme and commercial transmission system. With the modular elements outlined, a phased integration has been possible. An all digital distribution system offers improved operational simplicity without any of the day to day adjustments that are necessary with its analogue counterpart. In addition, the ability to distribute and record and large numbers of stereo sources each with its own source identification and integral time code, together with other user information offer considerable system benefits. It is believed that in spite of the technical difficulties that are still to be resolved, the move towards a totally digital distribution system is the way forward. Both the NICAM 728 and AES formats have been proved to be rugged and offer a high level of signal integrity. The adoption of these formats ensures total compatibility with the next generation of transmission standards that will find their way into terrestrial and satellite broadcast centres.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: NICAM television sound and the consumer
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Stereo Sound for Television
abstract: The requirements for introducing commercially successful consumer products are presented. The developments in television sound are reviewed. The expectations of users are analyzed in terms of product and service features.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Networking and transmission of dual channel sound
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Stereo Sound for Television
abstract: The introduction of NICAM digital sound has involved changes to the entire broadcast chain from the originating studio, through the distribution networks to transmitting station systems and also to the viewers home reception equipment. The paper describes the 'all digital' approach adopted by the IBA in the conversion of the network and transmitter systems for ITV and Channel 4 and highlights some of the novel techniques that have been employed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experience with NICAM 728 system in the Nordic countries
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Stereo Sound for Television
abstract: In January 1987, after two years of technical tests and experimental transmission the decision was taken to recommend a slightly modified version of the BBC system to be used for multichannel television sound transmissions in the Nordic countries. This recommendation was followed by the adoption of 'NICAM 728' by the EBU in April of the same year. This specification has subsequently become a draft CCIR recommendation. The first regular services with the NICAM 728 system started in Finland on January 8, 1988 followed by the start of the Swedish Network on February 27. Later the same year in October 1988 a new commercial Danish television network (TV2) started with all their transmitters broadcasting NICAM 728 stereo sound.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
